passage: The class had two weeks to build a volcano poster, and by Thursday Karthik had done most of it while Asif and Meera chatted. His jaw was tight. Instead of sulking he said, "This isn't working for me. Can we split the jobs? Asif, the fact cards. Meera, the labels." Meanwhile Aadhya, who had been handed only the glue, spoke up. "I have an idea for the title, and I could draw the map. Can I have a bigger job?" The others blinked, then agreed. Asif's fact cards came out messy, and after school Karthik stayed late to fix them without a word of complaint. When Asif saw the neat cards, he felt grateful and a bit guilty. "Thanks for fixing them, Karthik. I will do the next section properly," he said, and he did. On Monday, before the presentation, Karthik asked the teacher, "Could you look at our project notebook to see who did which part?" He described the facts calmly: names, tasks, days. He did not say anyone was lazy. The teacher nodded and wrote each name beside a task. 🙂

qa.q: What was the group building for class?
qa.a: They were building a volcano poster.

qa.q: How did Karthik's way of dealing with unequal work differ from Aadhya's way of dealing with tiny jobs?
qa.a: Karthik, whose jaw was tight, calmly asked to split the jobs, while Aadhya, who was handed only the glue, offered an idea for the title and asked for the map and a bigger job.

qa.q: How did Asif feel when he saw the neat cards, and why?
qa.a: He felt grateful and a bit guilty, because Karthik had stayed late to fix them without complaining.

qa.q: What could Asif keep doing to keep the team fair?
qa.a: He could keep doing his share properly and on time, and keep saying thank you clearly.

grounding: One school group shows unequal work: a member who did most, a member given tiny jobs, thanks for a stayed-late fix, and calmly asking the teacher who did what.

passage: After the incident on the office trip, Nitin filed a complaint. Months later HR told him the matter was closed, and his team lead moved him to a smaller desk. It felt like being harmed twice. He kept the emails, dates and the reply letter in a folder, and asked the internal committee for a written review. At night his body stayed on alert; every car door made him jolt awake, and sleep came in pieces. He blamed himself, for going on the trip at all and for still being a mess. "It has been so long. I should be over it," he told his friend Arohi over tea. "You did nothing wrong, and healing keeps its own time," Arohi said, and stayed until he had finished talking. She helped him book a session with Gurleen, a counsellor, who explained that sleeplessness and jumpiness are common after frightening events and suggested keeping regular meal and walking times. The anger came in waves after that. Nitin used it to write a firm email about his boundaries at work and to ask a helpline about proper next steps, instead of quitting in a rage.

qa.q: What did Nitin keep in a folder?
qa.a: He kept the emails, dates and the reply letter.

qa.q: How did Arohi's response to Nitin's self-blame differ from what the institution did with his complaint?
qa.a: HR closed the matter and his team lead moved him to a smaller desk, which felt like being harmed twice, while Arohi told him it was not his fault and stayed until he finished talking.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling when he said he should be over it?
qa.a: He felt ashamed, blaming himself for still struggling.

qa.q: What did Nitin do with his anger, and why is that wiser than quitting in a rage?
qa.a: He wrote a firm email about his boundaries and asked a helpline about proper next steps, which protects him and uses proper channels instead of harming himself further.

grounding: One person's aftermath of a frightening event shows an institution that ignored the complaint, shame, an alert body and anger turned toward boundaries.

passage: When Arnav ended it by text, Neelam felt hollow. She replayed their last chat until late at night and told herself she must be worthless if he could walk away so easily. Her friend Ganga sat beside her at lunch and got her to eat half a paratha. Neelam's anger arrived the next week; she wanted Arnav to hurt as she did. She wrote a furious page in her notebook, tore it out, then ran laps round the school ground. She did not post or send anything. She kept her sleep routine, and let herself cry. A week later, a screenshot of her private messages with Arnav went around the class group with a cruel caption. Neelam went cold. She did not reply. She saved the screenshot and the sender's name and showed her mother, Aditi, who held her hand and said, "Sharing your messages was a real breach of trust, and none of it is on you." The next morning they went to the school counsellor, who took it to the principal that same day, and the school contacted the cyber cell helpline. Neelam sat between Ganga and Aditi, shaking but supported.

qa.q: What did Ganga get Neelam to eat at lunch?
qa.a: She got Neelam to eat half a paratha.

qa.q: How did Ganga support Neelam compared with how Aditi supported her?
qa.a: Ganga sat beside Neelam at lunch and got her to eat half a paratha, while Aditi held her hand, said sharing the messages was a breach of trust and none of it was on her, and went with her to the school counsellor.

qa.q: How did Neelam feel when Arnav ended it, and what did she tell herself?
qa.a: She felt hollow and rejected, and she told herself she must be worthless.

qa.q: How could Neelam's friend and mother keep supporting her in the coming weeks?
qa.a: They could keep sitting with her, sharing meals and staying close while the school and helpline deal with the screenshot.

grounding: After a breakup, a teen goes through hollow grief, anger she does not act on, a sense of rejection and the shame of her private messages being shared.

passage: In the changing room, some boys joked about Rafiq's height, and one called him "pocket size". Rafiq's ears went hot. He gave them no reaction, and when it happened again the next day he told his class teacher, who spoke to the boys. He kept comparing himself with both the tall boys and the late bloomers, until his older cousin told him, "Bodies grow at different speeds. Mine didn't move until much later." Rafiq shrugged, unsure, but began sleeping better. Across the corridor, Leela scrolled through fitness and beauty accounts every night and felt she had to change. One evening she noticed that most of them were selling something. "They want me to feel small so I will buy," she realised, and she unfollowed most of them. But the mirror still pulled at her; she checked it all day and thought about food constantly, feeling out of control. She told Pema, the school counsellor, who listened, said that asking for help is brave, and phoned Leela's parents that afternoon so they could see a doctor together.

qa.q: What did one boy call Rafiq in the changing room?
qa.a: He called Rafiq "pocket size".

qa.q: How did Rafiq's handling of the mockery differ from Leela's handling of the influencer accounts?
qa.a: Rafiq gave no reaction and told his class teacher when the jokes were repeated, while Leela noticed that most of the accounts were selling something and unfollowed most of them.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling about her body and food when she went to Pema?
qa.a: She felt inadequate and out of control, since she checked the mirror all day and thought about food constantly.

qa.q: What could Leela do next after Pema phoned her parents?
qa.a: She could see a doctor together with her parents and keep talking with Pema, since asking for help early is a strength.

grounding: Four teens meet body worries: mockery about height, comparing puberty, influencers that sell inadequacy, and an obsession with mirrors and food.

passage: When baby Ojas came home, visitors crowded round the cot with gifts, and Lavanya stood at the edge with her hands behind her back. "Send him back," she muttered, and pinched his blanket hard. Sonali gently loosened her fingers. "You are angry. I understand. Hands stay soft with the baby, but you can stomp as loudly as you like." Lavanya stomped. Sonali kept Lavanya's bedtime the same and asked her to choose Ojas's socks. Some days later Sonali was worn out and juggling the baby's feeds, and Lavanya began talking in baby talk and clinging to her leg. That night Sonali set a timer for ten minutes and gave Lavanya her whole attention: they built a block house, no phone. "You are still my big one and my little one," Sonali said, "and there is room for both of you." Lavanya's shoulders relaxed. On Saturday she stroked Ojas's tiny hand and whispered, "His fingers are so small!" and ran to fetch a nappy. An hour later she frowned and wanted him off Mummy's lap, and Sonali said, "Both feelings are allowed."

qa.q: What did Lavanya mutter when the visitors crowded round the cot?
qa.a: She muttered, "Send him back."

qa.q: How did Lavanya's behaviour change between when Sonali was worn out and after the ten minutes of attention?
qa.a: When Sonali was busy, Lavanya used baby talk and clung to her leg; after ten minutes of full attention and hearing that there is room for both, her shoulders relaxed and she tenderly stroked Ojas's hand.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling when she said "Send him back"?
qa.a: She felt jealous, invisible and angry as the visitors crowded round the baby.

qa.q: What could Sonali keep doing to help Lavanya feel secure?
qa.a: She could keep the daily ten minutes of full attention, keep Lavanya's routine, and keep giving her small jobs with the baby. 🙂

grounding: A big sister meets a new baby with jealousy, regression when her mother is tired, reassurance that both children fit in the family, and tender love.

passage: Some classmates giggled at Pallavi's long braid, her prayer beads and the way she closed her eyes for a moment before lunch. "Weird," one whispered. Pallavi's face went hot with shame, but she told her teacher, who talked to the class about respect, and she leaned on her friend Abhinav, who said, "I like your beads." A week later Manoj, an elder in her family, said at dinner that people of Abhinav's faith were all bad. Pallavi frowned, thinking of how Abhinav shared his snack. She did not shout. She asked quietly, "Why do you think so?" and Manoj waved the question away. On Sunday Abhinav invited her to his festival. He explained each thing patiently, the lamps, the sweets, the songs, and she felt welcome. She joined in with folded hands, without changing what she believed herself. On Monday, when a classmate laughed at Abhinav's festival clothes and called his religion silly, Pallavi's heart pounded. She stood up. "That is not kind. It is his religion, and it is not silly." The classmate went quiet.

qa.q: What did Abhinav explain at his festival?
qa.a: He explained the lamps, the sweets and the songs.

qa.q: How did Pallavi's response to Manoj's remark differ from her response to the classmate's insult?
qa.a: With Manoj she asked quietly why Manoj thought so and held on to her own experience of Abhinav, while with the classmate she stood up and said the remark was not kind.

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel when the classmates giggled at her beads and braid?
qa.a: She felt ashamed, with her face going hot.

qa.q: What could Pallavi do if the mocking of her prayer continues?
qa.a: She could tell her teacher again and keep leaning on friends like Abhinav and on family who love her.

grounding: A child meets mockery of her own prayer, an elder's prejudice about a friend's faith, a friend's patient welcome to his festival, and defends his dignity.
